prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of atoms, enabling timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock meets the test I apply to every candidate: a specific original invention, experimentally verified, that opened a door to phenomena nobody could measure before. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift that would otherwise destroy the spectroscopy of many trapped atoms, and he made the first strontium demonstration. Ye's group then took the concept to the 10^-18 regime and used it for clock comparisons and many-body physics. The result has been reproduced and compared by independent laboratories in several countries, and it now supports tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the discussion of redefining the second. Seven of eight members ranked it, four of them first, and the two credited names are identical in every ballot, so the attribution question is unusually clean. I want this to rest on the historical record of who did the original experiment, and here that record is short and well localized.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize must be carefully separated from earlier frequency-metrology awards (Hall and Hansch 2005, Wineland and Haroche 2012), so the citation has to name the lattice-trapping invention itself and not clocks or frequency combs in general. A second concern is that other groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, and the strontium-clock work around Ludlow and Ye's JILA colleagues) contributed essential accuracy work, and a two-person prize cannot reflect that. Finally, the second has not yet been redefined, so someone could argue the practical payoff is still ahead; I do not find that persuasive, because the discovery criterion is the verified invention, not the downstream decision of the metrology bodies.

responses.point: Johansson puts circuit QED first as a clean, foundational demonstration that supplies the readout and coupling architecture of nearly every superconducting processor, and he ranks the lattice clock only fourth.
responses.response: I agree the circuit QED architecture is real and widely reproduced; I ranked it second myself. But I would resist placing it above the clock on originality of a single decisive result. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes the neighbouring field sensitive, and the credit problem is more severe: you note yourself that Blais is left out of a trio, and I think that exclusion is hard to defend since he led the 2004 proposal. The clock has two names that nobody disputes. If the committee prefers circuit QED, I would want the experimental and theoretical leads settled before we commit, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks topological insulators first, as a clear before-and-after discovery, and places IceCube second, while putting optical lattice clocks fifth because Ye's earlier comb connection is only indirect.
responses.response: I take the point that topological insulators are a deep conceptual discovery, but the attribution problem you identify yourself is the reason I cannot support it as the lead. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realization, and Hasan's 3D photoemission work is a separate claim, so three names cannot honestly cover both the 2D and 3D stories. As someone who must be absolutely sure we have the people who did the original work, I am not there yet for B004. On IceCube we agree it is a genuine new window; I ranked it third and keep it as an alternative, but I would want the source-identification evidence, which is at about three sigma for TXS 0506+056, to be weighed against the robust diffuse-flux discovery. On the clock, Ye's role is not indirect: his group delivered the accuracy and comparisons that made the invention matter.

responses.point: Pearce ranks optical lattice clocks first as a new measurement technique with careful systematics and agrees the citation must be separated from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, but also rates IceCube second and treats its credit as intrinsically difficult.
responses.response: We agree on both the ranking and the need to separate the citation from earlier prizes, and I have worded my proposed citation to name magic-wavelength lattice trapping specifically. On IceCube I share your concern about a large collaboration: Halzen conceived the project, Karle built a central part of the detector, but whether Yoshida or others deserve credit is exactly the question I cannot settle from the record. That uncertainty is why I put IceCube as an alternative rather than as a second prize part. Since the clock needs only two names, I do not see a need to attach a second achievement to make the prize work.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first on the strength of the Bistritzer-MacDonald theory paired with the Jarillo-Herrero experiments, while ranking the lattice clock fourth.
responses.response: The twisted bilayer story is a clean theory-plus-experiment pair and I ranked it fourth. My reservation is maturity: the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, and Dean, Young, Yazdani and others contributed key verifying experiments, so the credit may still be moving. I am also wary that the discovery is eight years old and the interpretation is not settled. That does not make it unworthy, but it is less secure than a result confirmed by independent laboratories at the 10^-18 level with agreeing comparisons.

uncertainties: Whether the citation can be worded so that it is clearly distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
How much weight to give the accuracy work of other groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST) when the credit is limited to two names.
For circuit QED, whether Blais or Girvin should be excluded from a three-person prize, and how close it sits to the 2025 prize.
For IceCube, whether the source-identification evidence is mature enough and whether Halzen, Karle and Yoshida are the right names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the clock candidate. I note that my colleague Goran Johansson is also in the Chalmers physics department and works on superconducting circuits, so I treat my views on circuit QED (B028) with some care, though I have no personal or institutional tie to any of the credited individuals as far as the profile shows.
